title: Next-generation GTR/GBR membranes: synergistic effects of nano-hydroxyapatite and vitamin D 3  on osteoinduction and scaffold performance
abstract: Abstract To develop a multifunctional membrane for guided tissue/bone regeneration (GTR/GBR), this study investigated the effect of incorporating nano‑hydroxyapatite (nHA) and vitamin D3 (VitD3) into electrospun polylactic acid (PLA) on scaffold properties and bone regeneration performance. Electrospun PLA/nHA-VitD3 membranes were fabricated and compared with neat PLA and a commercial membrane. Fiber morphology and porosity, water contact angle, tensile properties, and VitD3 release over 28 days were evaluated. In vitro performance was assessed using MG‑63 osteoblast viability and mineralization potential, while in vivo efficacy was examined in a rabbit calvarial defect model after 8 weeks. The PLA/nHA–VitD3 membranes exhibited reduced fiber diameter ( ~ 745 vs ~1039 nm) and higher porosity ( ~ 90% vs ~81%) compared with PLA, along with improved surface wettability (contact angle from 152° to 137%). Mechanical performance was enhanced, with tensile strength increasing from 0.10 ± 0.02 to 0.21 ± 0.05 MPa, Young’s modulus from 1.48 ± 0.3 to 15.1 ± 3.6 MPa, and elongation at break from 21% to 46%. VitD3 release from the composite membrane was sustained over 28 days ( ~ 85% cumulative release) without an initial burst. In vitro results showed increased MG‑63 cell viability ( ~ 1.8‑fold vs PLA at day 5) together with evidence of mineralization potential. In addition, osteogenic gene expression analysis showed upregulation of COL1A and RUNX2 in cells cultured on the PLA/nHA-VitD3 membrane, indicating enhanced early osteogenic activity. In the rabbit calvarial model, PLA/nHA-VitD3 membranes promoted ~82% new bone formation at 8 weeks, compared with ~54% for PLA and ~65% for the commercial membrane, with complete defect bridging and minimal inflammatory response. Overall, the incorporation of nHA and VitD3 improved the structural, mechanical, and biological performance of electrospun PLA membranes and contributed to enhanced bone regeneration, supporting their potential use as GBR/GTR barrier membranes. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Periodontitis is a long-term inflammatory condition characterized by the gradual breakdown of periodontal structures, potentially leading to tooth loss. To restore and reconstruct the affected periodontal tissues, two main surgical approaches guided tissue regeneration (GTR) and guided bone regeneration (GBR) are commonly employed [ 1 ,  2 ]. Both scenarios include using an occlusive membrane to inhibit the development of connective and epithelial tissues into the injured area, thereby facilitating periodontal tissue regeneration [ 3 ]. The membranes used in GTR/GBR play a crucial role in providing support for tissue regeneration. These membranes must possess certain qualities to facilitate optimal healing [ 4 ]. Successful integration of membranes into tissues without triggering inflammatory responses requires biocompatibility.

Additionally, they must have a degradation profile that matches tissue regeneration [ 5 ]. It is also essential that their mechanical and physical properties are appropriate for their use in vivo as barriers to inhibit the growth of epithelial and connective tissues. The surgical instruments should also resist tearing and rupture during surgery [ 6 ]. Furthermore, membrane porosity is necessary for cellular adaptation and sufficient nutrient permeation. Additionally, the membrane and bone graft should be osteoconductive [ 7 ]. Osteoconductivity is the capacity of a membrane or scaffold to promote osteoblast development from the edges of existing bones, resulting in the formation of new bone structures [ 8 ].

The requirement for all these properties restricts the selection of membranes depending on the GTR/GBR application. Non-resorbable membranes were previously used, but they required surgical intervention for removal after healing. Unlike traditional non-resorbable membranes, resorbable membranes undergo degradation over time and do not necessitate surgical removal [ 9 ]. Various synthetic polymers can be used, such as polylactic acid (PLA) [ 10 ], poly (glycolic acid) (PGA) [ 11 ], poly(caprolactone) (PCL) [ 12 ], Polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) [ 13 ] or their copolymers. The polymers provide exceptional biocompatibility, manageable biodegradability, minimal stiffness, and processability, together with favorable drug encapsulation qualities [ 14 ].

In this study, membranes were prepared from PLA, PLA/ nano Hydroxy apatite (nHA), and a mixture of PLA/nHA containing vitamin D 3 . PLA possesses desirable properties for tissue engineering, including high biocompatibility, improved bioactivity, controlled degradation rate, and non-toxic degradation products [ 15 ]. Hydroxyapatite (HA) is a traditional bone substitute because of its chemical composition and crystal structure, similar to calcium and Phosphorus in bone tissue [ 16 ]. A low absorption rate and trabecular structure of HA material promote the induction of blood and bone cells, which explains its excellent biocompatibility and osteoconductivity [ 17 ]. Nevertheless, the substrate of HA material on which osteoblasts are grown has a more significant influence on their proliferation and differentiation than HA itself. The high brittleness and low fracture toughness of pure HA make it unsuitable for bone regeneration. Thus, researchers have focused on modifying HA morphologically and functionally by combining it with synthesized polymers [ 18 ]. At the nanoscale, hydroxyapatite particles more closely mimic the size and morphology of native bone mineral, increasing their specific surface area and reactivity. Nano-hydroxyapatite (nHA) can provide abundant calcium and phosphate ion release and present bioactive sites for protein adsorption, thereby enhancing osteoblast adhesion, spreading, and focal adhesion formation [ 19 ]. Moreover, the nanostructured topography of nHA-containing scaffolds has been reported to stimulate osteogenic differentiation and osteoconductive behavior by modulating cell–material interactions and cytoskeletal organization [ 20 ,  21 ].

Vitamin D is a steroid hormone acquired mainly by sun exposure, diet, and dietary supplements [ 22 ]. Vitamin D 3  (VitD 3 ) is explicitly considered in implantology since it affects immune function and bone metabolism. This prohormone’s impact positively correlates with the osseointegration process at the proper concentration. According to research, VitD 3  has a significant role in the healing of postoperative wounds, the osseointegration of dental implants, and the maintenance of bone homeostasis around the implant [ 23 ]. Upon binding to its nuclear vitamin D receptor (VDR), VitD 3  regulates the transcription of several osteogenic genes and modulates osteoblast differentiation. VDR-mediated signaling upregulates key osteoblast markers, including runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and osteocalcin, thereby promoting matrix maturation and mineralization [ 24 ]. In addition, VitD3 has been shown to enhance the expression of bone morphogenetic proteins and integrins, which can further support osseointegration and bone–implant interface stability [ 23 ].

GTR/GBR scaffolds can exhibit a wide range of properties depending on their fabrication and morphology. Scaffold porosity is one of the most important parameters affecting tissue regeneration [ 25 ]. Scaffold porosity and pore size are critical design parameters for successful GTR/GBR membranes, as they govern cell infiltration, nutrient transport, and neovascularization. Previous studies have suggested that interconnected pores in the range of approximately 100–500 µm are favorable for osteoblast migration and new bone formation. In addition, an overall porosity typically above 70–80% has been associated with improved bone ingrowth, provided that sufficient mechanical stability is maintained [ 26 ].

Traditionally, scaffolds were made from porous foam using conventional methods such as solvent casting, gas foaming, or particulate leaching [ 27 ]. Electrospinning has recently been introduced as an easy, reproducible method of preparing thin fibrous membranes. Compared to other scaffold types, electrospun fibers provide a large surface area, promoting osteoblastic cell function and bone regeneration [ 28 ,  29 ]. Furthermore, nanofibers have pores smaller than cells, so they can act as a barrier preventing connective and epithelial cells from penetrating [ 30 ].

In this work, we developed electrospun nanofibrous membranes composed of poly(lactic acid) (PLA), nano-hydroxyapatite (nHA), and vitamin D 3  (VitD 3 ) for guided tissue and bone regeneration applications. The design integrates the biocompatibility and biodegradability of PLA with the osteoconductive features of nHA and the bioactive role of VitD 3  in enhancing bone regeneration and osseointegration. The fabricated scaffolds were systematically prepared and assessed for their physicochemical and mechanical properties, as well as their potential to support periodontal tissue regeneration. This study presents a new class of multifunctional GTR/GBR scaffolds that unite structural reinforcement with localized bioactivity, offering a promising approach for advanced regenerative therapies.

sections.heading: Materials and reagents
paragraphs: Polylactic acid (PLA, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol, ≥98% purity, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), and paraformaldehyde (PFA, 4% aqueous solution, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) were used as received. Chloroform, acetone, and dimethylformamide (DMF) (analytical grade, Merck, Germany) and Alizarin Red S staining solution (Merck, Germany) were employed as solvents and staining reagents. Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM-high glucose), fetal bovine serum (FBS), penicillin (100 U/mL), and streptomycin (100 µg/mL) were purchased from Bioidea (Tehran, Iran) and used before their expiration dates.

sections.heading: Preparation of electrospun PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA/ VitD 3  fibers
paragraphs: As the first step, PLA solution with 5% wt concentration was prepared in chloroform:acetone volume ratio of 8:2. Afterwards, the PLA/ nHA solution was prepared in these solvents at a 5%wt polymer concentration and 5%(w/v) nHA for 30 minutes. After that, VitD 3  with 3%(w/w) of polymer concentration dissolved in DMF and the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  were electrospun with chloroform: DMF with 8:2 volume ratio. For prepared scaffolds with this method, the fibers were electrospun with a needle diameter of 0.6 mm at a feed rate of 1 mL/h. Also, the distance of the collector to the needle was 18 cm, and the voltage was 20-25 kV  [ 31 ,  32 ].

sections.heading: Chemical structure and morphological evaluation
paragraphs: The chemical bonds and functional groups of scaffolds were assessed using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). Observations of infrared beam absorption peaks have been performed at 400 to 4000 cm −1  wavelengths. An X-ray Diffraction (XRD) analysis has been conducted using the D8ADVANCE Model by Bruker in Germany to determine the scaffolds’ crystallinity, interatomic distances, and lattice parameters. The study was conducted using a copper (Cu) anode X-ray tube with a wavelength of 1.540598 °A (Cu Kα). A nickel (Ni) filter was used, and the angle between 2θ ranged from 5° to 75°. The count time was set at 1° per minute, and the step size was 0.05. The analysis was performed at room temperature. The percentage of crystallinity for each scaffold was calculated using the peak fitting technique. In this approach, distinct peaks indicate areas of crystalline structure, whereas the remaining peaks indicate regions that lack a defined crystalline structure. Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM, Philips, XL30) was used to assess fiber shape, fiber diameters, and porosity. Before SEM imaging, the samples were coated with a layer of gold using a sputtering technique. Subsequently, the Image-J Software (Version 1.52 v, USA) utilized a random selection method to choose 25 fibers and determine the mean diameter of such fibers. The porosity % is also assessed using the MATLAB software [ 33 ]. Elemental analysis was performed using Electron diffraction X-ray (EDX, TESCAN, Germany) spectroscopy.

sections.heading: Evaluation of water wettability, swelling, and degradation ratio
paragraphs: W 2  shows the weight of the sample when it is swollen, whereas W 1  describes the weight of the sample when it is dry.
In this equation, W₂ denotes the weight of the sample after degradation at specific time intervals, while W₁ refers to the initial weight of the sample prior to immersion in PBS.

sections.heading: Vitamin D 3  release
paragraphs: In order to assess drug release from PLA/nHA–VitD 3  fibers, samples (2.5 × 2.5 cm 2 ) were immersed in 10 mL of PBS (n = 3). Afterwards, the samples were placed in a shaker incubator for 24 hours to assess drug entrapment efficiency. Furthermore, the samples (in PBS) were incubated at 37 °C for 28 days. At predetermined time intervals, an aliquot of the release medium was withdrawn and replaced with fresh PBS, and the amount of released VitD 3  was quantified by UV–Vis spectrophotometry (Shimadzu, Japan) at 265 nm.

The quantitative analysis of VitD 3  in the release medium was carried out using a UV–Vis spectrophotometer (Shimadzu, Japan) at 265 nm. The analytical method was validated prior to sample analysis. Selectivity was confirmed by recording the spectra of blank PBS, PLA/nHA scaffolds without VitD 3 , and VitD3-free degradation media under the same experimental conditions; no significant absorbance was observed at 265 nm for these controls, indicating negligible interference from PLA degradation products, nHA, or other components of the system.

For calibration, a series of VitD 3  standard solutions were prepared in PBS covering the expected concentration range in the release study. The calibration curve showed good linearity with a correlation coefficient (R²) of ≥ 0.999. Method precision was evaluated by repeated analysis of a quality control solution at low, medium, and high concentrations within the calibration range on the same day (intra-day) and on three consecutive days (inter-day). The encapsulation efficiency and cumulative release of VitD 3  were calculated using the validated calibration curve.
The drug release percentages presented in this study were therefore calculated based on the actual amount of drug incorporated in the membranes.

sections.heading: Mechanical behavior
paragraphs: The mechanical characteristics of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  were evaluated using a tensile test conducted with a Hounsfield machine equipped with a 50 N load cell, following the ASTM D638 standard. The 30 mm×10 mm scaffolds were cut and subjected to tensile stress. The strain rate was maintained at a constant 10 mm/min. The obtained stress–strain curves were used to determine the tensile strength, elongation at break, and elastic modulus, which corresponds to the slope of the curve within its linear region.

sections.heading: In vitro bioactivity evaluation
paragraphs: According to ISO 10993-18, PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds were cut into 1 × 1 cm² samples and immersed in 10 mL of simulated body fluid (SBF) for 28 days. The samples were incubated at a controlled temperature of 37°C. Throughout the study, the pH of the SBF was monitored weekly and maintained between 7.42 and 7.45. At 14 and 28-day intervals, the scaffolds were removed, rinsed with distilled water, and examined for surface morphology using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Following scaffold removal, calcium and phosphorus concentrations in the SBF were analyzed using inductively coupled plasma–optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES, Agilent 5110, USA) [ 36 ].

sections.heading: In vitro cell assay
paragraphs: To evaluate the adhesion and spreading of L929 and MG-63 cells on the membrane surfaces, the samples were rinsed with PBS and fixed with 1.5% glutaraldehyde at 4°C for 4 hours, three days after cell seeding. Subsequently, the cells were dehydrated through a graded ethanol series and then air-dried. Prior to scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging, the specimens were coated with a thin layer of gold under vacuum conditions. Imaging was performed using a Philips SEM system .

sections.heading: Gene expression
paragraphs: MG‑63 osteoblast‑like cells were seeded onto the membrane samples (n = 3 per group) in 12‑well plates at a density of 1×10⁵ cells/mL. After 7 days of culture, total RNA was extracted using a commercial RNA isolation kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA concentration and purity were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA), and samples with A260/A280 ratios between 1.8 and 2.1 were used for downstream analysis. Subsequently, 1 µg of RNA from each sample was reverse‑transcribed into cDNA using a first‑strand cDNA synthesis kit.

Quantitative real‑time PCR (qRT‑PCR) was performed using a SYBR Green master mix on a Bio‑Rad real‑time PCR detection system (Hercules, CA, USA). GAPDH was used as the internal reference gene. Primer sequences for RUNX2, COL1A, and GAPDH are provided in Table  1 . The thermal cycling protocol consisted of an initial denaturation at 95°C for 3 minutes, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 10 seconds and annealing/extension at 60°C for 30 seconds. A melt‑curve analysis was conducted at the end of each run to verify primer specificity and the absence of nonspecific products. Table 1 Specific primers for real-time PCR Gene Primer sequence (forward) Primer sequence (reverse) Col1A TCTACCCCCCTCTTCACTCTTC CTCTTACTTCCTCCCACCCCA RUNX2 CCGCACGACAACCGCACCAT CGCTCCGGCCCACAAATCTC GAPDH AGGTCGGTGTGAACGGATTTG TGTAGACCATGTAGTTGAGGTCA
Relative gene expression levels were calculated using the 2  - ∆∆Ct  method, where ΔC t  = Ct  gene  – Ct  GAPDH , and ΔΔC t  = ΔCt  gene  – ΔCt  control  [ 37 ].

sections.heading: Surgical procedure
paragraphs: Twelve adult male New Zealand white rabbits, each weighing between 2 and 2.5 kg, were procured from the Pasteur Institute in Tehran, Iran. The animals were housed under standardized conditions in an animal facility, maintained at a temperature of 20–25°C with a 12-hour light/dark cycle, and had unrestricted access to food and water throughout the experiment. The experimental protocol was approved by the Animal Use and Care Committee of Isfahan University of Medical Sciences (Ethics Code: IR.MUI.RESEARCH.REC.1399.646), and all procedures complied with relevant institutional and national guidelines.

Prior to surgery, anesthesia was induced via intraperitoneal injection of ketamine (90 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/kg). The surgical area on the head was cleaned using iodophor and alcohol after shaving. Animals were secured in a thoracic surgical position, and a 5 cm midline incision was made on the scalp. Once the fascia was retracted, the skull was exposed, and three full-thickness critical-size defects (8 mm in diameter) were created in the central calvarial region using a surgical trephine drill under continuous saline irrigation at low rotational speed. The scaffold dimensions (1 cm diameter, 500μm thickness) were selected based on the critical-size defect criteria for rabbit calvaria.

Circular scaffolds made of PLA, PLA/nHA, PLA/nHA-VitD 3 , and commercial materials were implanted into the defects, while one group served as the untreated control. For comparative evaluation, a commercially available biomaterial, Tatu‑Patch (Prodentis GmbH, Germany), was used as a reference membrane. After implantation, the skin was sutured using 4-0 silk, and the surgical site was disinfected and treated with tetracycline spray to enhance healing. Postoperative care included administration of analgesics and antibiotics for seven days: tramadol (10 mg/kg, subcutaneous; 50 mg/mL ampoule, AGLOBAL CARE, Philippines) and enrofloxacin (5 mg/kg, intramuscular; Enrofan 5%, Erfan, Tehran, Iran). Following surgery, each rabbit was placed in an individual cage and transferred to the recovery facility for monitoring. All animals were sacrificed at a single endpoint, 8 weeks after membrane implantation in the calvarial defect model. No interim euthanasia or sampling was performed; thus, all histological, histomorphometric, and analysis data correspond to the 8-week post-implantation timepoint.

sections.heading: Histological analysis
paragraphs: For histological analysis, explanted calvarial specimens were fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin for 48 hours and subsequently decalcified in 10% nitric acid for approximately two weeks. The decalcification protocol was selected due to its ability to achieve complete mineral removal within a practical timeframe for dense cranial tissue, allowing consistent sectioning without compromising general tissue morphology. Although nitric acid is a strong decalcifying agent, the concentration and exposure duration were optimized to preserve cellular and extracellular matrix structures for routine histological evaluation. After decalcification, samples were dehydrated through a graded ethanol series (80–100%), cleared in toluene, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 5 μm thickness. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed for qualitative assessment of tissue organization, inflammatory response, fibrous tissue formation, and new bone matrix deposition. Alizarin Red staining was used to qualitatively identify residual mineralized deposits and mineralized matrix areas that may remain detectable following controlled decalcification.
Histological sections were examined using a light microscope at magnifications of ×40 and ×100, and representative images were captured for further analysis.

Three histological sections were selected from each specimen in all experimental groups (PLA, PLA/nHA, PLA/nHA‑VitD3, commercial scaffolds, and control). The sections were analyzed under a light microscope at 100× magnification, and a minimum of six images were randomly captured per section. Quantitative analysis was performed to assess the percentages of newly formed bone, remaining graft material, and connective tissue. Histomorphometric data were obtained using ImageJ software, developed by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Maryland, USA. To ensure consistency in the histological evaluation, sections were obtained from the central region of the calvarial defect. For each specimen, multiple sections were prepared and examined, and representative images were selected from comparable anatomical regions of the defect area. This approach was used to minimize variability and ensure consistent comparison among the experimental groups.

sections.heading: Statistical analysis
paragraphs: All measurements in this study were performed in triplicate (n = 3). The resulting data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by the Tukey–Kramer post hoc test to determine statistical significance. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism software (version 9).

sections.heading: Characterization of PLA, PLA/nHA, PLA/nHA-VitD 3
paragraphs: In this study, PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  membranes were fabricated and evaluated as candidate GTR/GBR scaffolds for dental applications. Figure  1  A shows the FTIR spectra of PLA, nHA, VitD 3 , PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3 . The FTIR spectrum of PLA revealed characteristic peaks corresponding to the C–O–C stretching vibration at 1078 cm⁻¹, the carbonyl (C = O) group at 1754 cm⁻¹, and CH₃ stretching at 2997 cm⁻¹[ 39 ,  40 – 41 ]. In the PLA/nHA spectrum, additional peaks were observed within the 600–3000 cm⁻¹ range, indicating the presence of various functional groups. Notably, a broad OH stretching peak appeared at 3574 cm⁻¹, CH₃ vibrations were detected at 1629 cm⁻¹, and the PO₄³⁻ group was identified at 1380 cm⁻¹ [ 42 ,  43 ].
Fig. 1 ( A ) FTIR spectra of PLA, nHA, VitD 3 , PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  membranes, and ( B ) XRD spectra of nHA and PLA/nHA samples

The distinct peaks confirm the successful incorporation of both nHA and VitD 3  into the polymer matrix, suggesting strong chemical interactions that may influence degradation and release kinetics.. These included an N–H stretching vibration at 3396 cm⁻¹, a CH₂ group at 2926 cm⁻¹, and a C = O stretching band at 1640 cm⁻¹ [ 44 ].

Figure  1B  displays XRD patterns of nHA and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  membranes. According to previous studies, PLA has a prominent peak at 2ϴ = 20°-35°, associated with its semi-crystalline structure [ 45 ,  46 ]. As shown in Fig.  1B , the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  has a broad peak ranging from 2ϴ = 35° to 50°. Placing nHA molecules between PLA polymer chains and varying crystallinity (crystal size and distribution) forms this broad spectrum [ 47 ]. The XRD spectrum of nHA has peaks at 2ϴ = 26°, 31°, 39°, 45°, and 56°, which are related to the nHA planes (002), (211), (310), (222), and (213), respectively. The presence of nHA and VitD 3  has affected the broad prominent peak of the PLA to a sharper peak in the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  spectra. Furthermore, compared to the nHA sample, the crystalline nHA phase integrated into the polymer matrix occurs at almost the exact peak locations. This property indicates that the nHA dispersion in the matrix is highly uniform. Nonetheless, the effect can be reduced due to the low nHA amount of the matrix [ 48 ].

Figure  2  shows the surface morphologies of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  fibers. The PLA, PLA with HA, and fibers containing nHA and VitD 3  display a regular, uniform, and porous network structure. The fiber diameter distribution diagram was obtained by measuring the diameters of 25 fibers in the SEM images. The average fiber diameters for PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds were found to be 1039 ± 27 nm, 1403 ± 45 nm, and 745 ± 19 nm, respectively (P˂0.05). The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) results indicated that the inclusion of VitD 3  and nHA in the scaffold did not adversely affect the PLA fibres’ structure (diameter, surface morphology, etc.). Similarly, Shirzaei Sani et al. [ 49 ] evaluated the effect of HA on PCL fiber diameters and showed that the electrospinning fibers diameters and solution viscosity were increased by adding HA to the polymer structure. Also, Malla et al. [ 50 ] evaluated the effect of adding VitD 3  and nanoHA on PCL/PLA/Gelatin electrospun fibers and showed that by adding nano-HA to polymers composition, the diameters of the fibers increased, but after the addition of VitD 3  to this component (PCL/PLA/Gelatin-HA) the fiber diameters were decreased significantly.

Fig. 2 Morphological and elemental characterization of electrospun membranes. Representative SEM micrographs (left column) showing the fibrous morphology of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD3 ( scale bar  ~  40 µm ), SEM images combined with EDX elemental mapping (middle column) illustrate the elemental distribution within the membranes ( scale bar  ~  200 µm ). oxygen (blue), calcium (green) and phosphorus (red) signals, and histograms of fiber diameter distribution (right column) present the statistical analysis of fiber diameters for each membrane formulation

In addition, the average porosities for PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  GBR/GTR membranes were measured and revealed to be 81.16 ± 3.2%, 80.54 ± 6.9%, and 90.55 ± 2.8%, respectively. Indeed, the addition of VitD3 resulted in reduced fiber diameter but increased scaffold porosity, which may further promote nutrient and oxygen transport in tissue regeneration [ 51 ].

Elemental analysis of the membranes was further investigated using SEM‑EDX to confirm the presence and distribution of the inorganic phase within the electrospun fibers. In the PLA membrane, the elemental mapping mainly revealed blue signals corresponding to oxygen, which is consistent with the elemental composition of the PLA polymer matrix. The EDX spectrum also confirmed the presence of the characteristic elements of the polymer backbone.

In contrast, the PLA/nHA and PLA/nHA‑VitD3 membranes exhibited additional elemental signals corresponding to calcium and phosphorus, represented by green and red dots in the elemental maps, respectively. These signals originate from the hydroxyapatite nanoparticles incorporated within the fibrous structure. The elemental distribution maps demonstrated that calcium and phosphorus were homogeneously dispersed throughout the fibrous network without noticeable agglomeration. This uniform distribution indicates successful incorporation of nHA nanoparticles into the electrospun PLA matrix and suggests effective integration of the inorganic phase within the membrane structure.

sections.heading: Assessment of wettability, swelling behavior, and degradation profile
paragraphs: Water contact angle measurements (Fig.  3A ) were conducted to assess the surface wettability of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  membranes. Results indicated that incorporating nHA into PLA significantly reduced the contact angle, enhancing surface wettability. Specifically, the contact angle decreased from 152.28 ± 4° for pure PLA to 142.34 ± 5° for the PLA/nHA composite. The addition of VitD 3  further reduced the contact angle to 137.05 ± 2°. This improvement in wettability may be attributed to the reduction in fiber diameter and modifications in surface morphology. These findings suggest that scaffold wettability is governed by multiple factors, including chemical composition, surface roughness, porosity, and crystallinity [ 52 ]. Improved wettability is crucial for protein adsorption and initial cell adhesion, which are essential for osteoblast activity and subsequent bone regeneration.

Fig. 3 ( A ) Water contact angle measurements of the scaffolds,  B  swelling ratio,  C  weight loss over 56 days of in vitro degradation, and ( D)  cumulative release profile of VitD 3  from the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  membrane in PBS at 37°C over 28 days. All data are expressed as mean values (n = 3) ± standard deviation. Statistical significance is indicated as follows: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.005, ***P < 0.0005, ****P < 0.00005

In tissue engineering, water absorption and degradation behavior are critical features of biomaterials. To evaluate these properties, the swelling ratio and weight loss of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds were measured in phosphate-buffered saline at 37°C. The results are presented in Fig.  3 B and C. Figure  3B  shows that nHA and VitD₃ addition markedly increase scaffold water uptake. In fact, our PLA/nHA-VitD₃ membranes absorb ~33% more water than pure PLA. This improved hydrophilicity (lower contact angles) likely stems from nHA’s polar surfaces and the finer fiber morphology. Such an effect has been noted by others; for instance Guler et al. [ 53 ] observed the swelling capacity of the scaffold was increased by adding VitD 3 /VitK 2 /Mg 2+  ions to PLA/tricalcium phosphate/PCL composite nanofibers. They showed that by releasing VitD 3  and Vit K 2,  the water uptake capacity increases with the enhancement of nanofiber strength.

Usually, the regeneration of a bone defect requires 40 days, but it is sometimes delayed up to 6 months, depending on the severity of the defect and changing external conditions. Thus, a bone defect treatment material should persist to perform for no less than 40 days [ 54 ]. The biodegradability of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  fibrous scaffolds was assessed over a 60-day period in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). As shown in Fig.  3 C, the PLA scaffold exhibited the slowest rate of degradation, retaining approximately 95% of its original mass by day 60. In contrast, the PLA/nHA and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds showed greater degradation, retaining 80% and 85% of their initial weight, respectively. While the PLA/nHA showed a maximum weight loss over 60 days of incubation in PBS, the total rate of weight loss was relatively slow overall. The weight loss for the PLA scaffold demonstrated a consistent weight decrease over two months. A controlled degradation profile matching the bone healing timeline (40–60 days) is highly desirable for GTR/GBR membranes, and our PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds appear well aligned with this requirement. These findings are in line with other findings that have been reported [ 55 ]. Inversely, it was discovered that the degradation of the composite scaffolds (PLA/nHA and PLA/nHA-VitD 3 ) was non-uniform and showed two weight loss rates during the same period. There was a significant mass loss from 0 to 21 days. Similarly, Diaz et al. [ 56 ] evaluated a PCL/nHA scaffold prepared using the lyophilization technique and displayed a similarly recognizable weight loss curve during four weeks of degradation. On the other hand, Melnik et al. [ 57 ] found that adding nHA to PCL fibers accelerated degradation, likely due to release of Ca²⁺/PO₄³⁻ (they found faster mass loss and ion release than for PCL alone), leading to improved osteoconduction. Furthermore, it is conceivable that differences in the weight loss of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  are due to various fiber structures and morphologies.

A common challenge in GBR/GTR membranes is the rapid drug release caused by the presence of drugs on the membrane surface [ 4 ]. In this study, VitD 3  was encapsulated within hydrophobic polymers such as PLA and PLA/nHA to prevent burst release and sustained drug delivery. The encapsulation efficiency of vitamin D₃ in the PLA/nHA membranes was determined to be approximately 93 ± 4%, indicating efficient incorporation of the drug into the electrospun matrix. Therefore, the release profile presented in this study reflects the release behavior of the actual drug content within the membranes. As illustrated in Fig.  3D , the release profile of VitD 3  from the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffold over 28 days followed a linear trend, indicating a sustained and gradual release pattern. The rate of drug release is influenced by several parameters, including swelling behavior, degradation rate, and drug solubility in the surrounding medium [ 52 ].

The delayed release observed in the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  group may be attributed to the barrier effect of the PLA matrix, which limits the diffusion of both the medium and drug molecules through the scaffold. This interpretation is supported by the swelling and degradation analyses, which confirmed a controlled hydration and degradation pattern in all scaffold groups. Overall, these findings suggest that VitD 3 -loaded PLA/nHA fibers hold strong potential for long-term drug delivery applications.

sections.heading: Mechanical characteristics
paragraphs: For GBR/GTR membranes, possessing suitable mechanical properties such as high tensile strength and flexibility is crucial to withstand handling and facilitate insertion into target tissues during implantation [ 58 ]. Accordingly, the mechanical performance of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds was evaluated under dry conditions. Parameters measured included tensile strength, Young’s modulus, and elongation at break, as presented in Fig.  4 . The results showed that PLA had the lowest mechanical characteristics, with a tensile strength of 0.1 ± 0.02 MPa (Fig.  4B ) and a modulus of 1.48 ± 0.3 MPa (Fig.  4C ). Although the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffold’s modulus was significantly increased to 15.1 ± 3.6 MPa, and stress strength was enhanced to 0.21 ± 0.05 by the addition of nHA and VitD 3  in comparison with PLA. The modulus of ~15 MPa remains well below that of cortical bone ( ~ 1–2 GPa), but falls within the handling range reported for clinically used GBR membranes, suggesting sufficient mechanical integrity for barrier function during healing. However, compared to pure PLA (21.76 ± 4.9%), the elongation at break of PLA/nHA-VitD 3  fibers (46.2 ± 2.9%) increased. This improved elongation at break indicates reduced brittleness, which enhances clinical applicability by making the membranes easier to handle and suture without tearing during surgery. The influence of VitD 3  on fiber shape and the reduced fiber diameter, which enable the polymer to improve at higher elongations, are the causes of the enhancing elongation of PLA/HA-VitD 3  [ 59 ]. Similarly, Neto et al. [ 60 ] evaluated mechanical properties of PLA and PCL with different amounts of nHA were produced by electrospinning. The result showed that adding nHA to PCL and PLA fibers separately improved the young modulus and stress strength through increasing crystallite phases of fibers structure. In another study, Guler et al. [ 53 ] it was shown that adding VitD 3  to a composite fiber consisting of polylactic acid, tricalcium phosphate, and polycaprolactone increased its strength, which can be due to VitD 3  having crystalline structures. Consequently, their crystalline structures give them more strength for interacting with adsorbate molecules.

Fig. 4 ( A ) Tensile stress–strain curves of the membranes and corresponding quantitative analyses: ( B ) average tensile strength,  C  average elastic modulus, and ( D)  average elongation at break. All results are expressed as mean values (n = 3) ± standard deviation. Statistical significance is indicated as follows: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.005, ***P < 0.0005, ****P < 0.00005

The dramatic increase in tensile strength and Young’s modulus upon adding nHA mirrors previous observations that hydroxyapatite nanofillers reinforce polymer matrices. For instance, Custódio et al. [ 61 ] demonstrated that incorporating 15 wt% nano-HAp into 3D-printed PLA scaffolds increased tensile strength from ~32.7 MPa to ~47.3 MPa and modulus from ~2.3 GPa to ~3.5 GPa, highlighting the reinforcing role of nHA in polymer composites. Similarly, Bernardo et al. [ 62 ] reported that HAp nanoparticles significantly enhanced the mechanical stability of biodegradable membranes, thereby improving their suitability for GBR/GTR applications. Our findings that PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds exhibited higher tensile strength and modulus than pure PLA are consistent with these results, further supporting the beneficial effect of nHA loading.

sections.heading: Bioactivity assessment
paragraphs: Bioactivity assessment is a critical component in evaluating a material’s suitability for bone regeneration. One of the key roles of polymers in this context is their ability to support mineralization by promoting the deposition of calcium phosphate compounds. This process is often mediated by the interaction between the polymer and negatively charged functional groups such as carboxylates which facilitate hydroxyapatite nucleation when exposed to simulated body fluid (SBF). In this study, PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds were immersed in SBF for 28 days to investigate their mineralization potential. The formation of hydroxyapatite on the scaffold surfaces was examined via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and inductively coupled plasma (ICP) analysis.

To confirm surface crystallization following SBF immersion, SEM imaging was conducted at one, two, and four weeks post-incubation (Fig.  5A ). SBF is rich in calcium and phosphate ions, which can induce the formation of apatite-like crystals when interacting with bioactive materials. SEM images revealed the presence of calcium phosphate particles across all scaffold types; however, notable differences were observed in their morphology and density.

Fig. 5 ( A ) SEM images of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds after 7, 21, and 28 days of immersion in simulated body fluid (SBF), showing progressive apatite-like crystal formation on scaffold surfaces,  B  ICP analysis of calcium (Ca) ion concentration in SBF after incubation with different scaffolds for 28 days, and ( C)  ICP analysis of phosphorus (P) ion concentration in SBF after incubation with different scaffolds for 28 days

PLA, though a synthetic polymer, displays intrinsic bioactivity. Upon exposure to aqueous physiological environments, PLA undergoes surface hydrolysis, leading to the generation of carboxylic acid (–COOH) groups. These negatively charged groups interact electrostatically with Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ ions in the SBF, thereby facilitating the nucleation and deposition of hydroxyapatite crystals on the scaffold surface[ 63 ].

The incorporation of nHA and VitD 3  into the scaffolds significantly promoted the formation of spherical apatite-like crystals, especially at higher concentrations, as illustrated in Fig.  5A . The presence of nHA within the fibers increased surface roughness and provided abundant nucleation sites, thereby enhancing mineral deposition from the surrounding simulated body fluid. Nano-hydroxyapatite (nHA) is well-recognized for its excellent bioactivity and biocompatibility, largely due to its high surface area-to-volume ratio and strong osteoconductive properties, which support and accelerate bone tissue formation [ 19 ,  64 ].

As a result, these scaffold compositions appear highly suitable for bone tissue engineering applications, as they are capable of forming a bioactive apatite layer that can chemically bond with native bone tissue. In addition to the well-established role of nHA in promoting nucleation, the contribution of VitD 3  is also noteworthy [ 24 ]. SEM observations suggest that VitD 3  not only influences apatite crystal formation in vitro but may also play a role in enhancing bone regeneration in vivo.

The findings confirm that both PLA/nHA and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds exhibit bioactive surfaces capable of supporting hydroxyapatite formation. To further assess this property, the concentrations of calcium and phosphorus ions in the SBF solution were measured at the end of week four using inductively coupled plasma (ICP) analysis, as presented in Fig.  5 B and C. It is well established that as calcium phosphate layers begin to form on scaffold surfaces, the levels of calcium and phosphate ions in the surrounding medium typically decline over time [ 65 ,  66 ].

After 28 days, a substantial reduction in calcium concentration was observed in the PLA/nHA and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  groups compared to the PLA scaffold. Specifically, calcium ion depletion was approximately 30% for PLA, 60% for PLA/nHA, and 62% for PLA/nHA-VitD 3 . The higher Ca/P depletion observed in PLA/nHA and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds supports rapid nucleation, which is advantageous for establishing chemical bonds with native bone tissue. This suggests that the incorporation of nHA and VitD 3  provides favorable surface conditions that enhance calcium ion binding and apatite layer formation. Similarly, phosphorus ion concentrations decreased significantly over the 28-day period in the modified scaffolds. The reduction was approximately 18% for PLA, but markedly higher for PLA/nHA and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  at around 93% and 92%, respectively. These findings further support the role of nHA and VitD 3  in facilitating phosphate interaction and deposition on scaffold surfaces. Formation of an apatite-like layer is widely recognized as a predictor of in vivo osteointegration potential, reinforcing the translational relevance of these scaffolds for clinical bone regeneration. Consistent with prior research, the inclusion of nHA has been shown to promote natural hydroxyapatite formation by providing nucleation sites within the scaffold matrix [ 67 ].

sections.heading: Biocompatibility: cell viability and morphology
paragraphs: To evaluate the potential of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  as GBR/GTR membranes, a facile approach was first adopted to examine the scaffold cytocompatibility. As the most abundant cell type in the periodontal tissues, fibroblasts (L-929) and osteoblast (MG-63) cells are responsible for tissue regeneration. A direct method was utilized to assess the potentially toxic effects of the substances, using the MTT investigation (Fig.  6 A, B). Based on the results shown in Fig.  6 A and B, it can be observed that both L929 and MG63 cells exhibited a consistent and significant enhancement of their growth rate as the duration of culture increased, regardless of the substances they were in contact with. Furthermore, there was no noticeable presence of cytotoxic reactions. Based on the data shown in Fig.  6A , it can be concluded that there was no statistically significant difference between the PLA and PLA/nHA scaffolds (P > 0.05). The combination of VitD 3  and nHA in the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffold enhances bioactivity and surface morphology, creating an optimal environment for cell growth and proliferation. After five days of culturing L929 cells, the scaffolds containing nHA/VitD 3  showed a significant increase (P < 0.05) in cell viability, as shown in Fig.  6A . This enhancement may result from synergistic effects of nHA, which enhances bone cell prolifration, and VitD3, which provides favorable environment for bone regeneration, In addition, as shown in Fig.  6B , this process is visible in MG-63 cell line. In such a way that by adding nHA and VitD 3  to the structure and increasing the hydrophilicity, bioactivity, and changed surface morphology, after 3 and 5 days, the cell viability has increased significantly (P˂0.05). Such dual bioactivity suggests that PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds may accelerate early osseointegration in clinical settings.

Fig. 6 ( A ) Relative viability of L929 cells and ( B)  relative viability of MG63 cells cultured on different scaffold samples, assessed over 5 days using the MTT assay and normalized to the control group (TCP).  C  SEM images showing L929 and MG63 cell attachment and morphology on the surfaces of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds, captured three days after cell seeding. Data are presented as mean values (n = 3) ± standard deviation. Statistical significance is denoted as follows: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.005, ***P < 0.0005, ****P < 0.00005

In another study, the effect of HA on silicon dioxide (SiO 2 ) and hydroxyapatite (HAp) in the Polycaprolactone matrix has proven that the induction of L929 and MG-63 cell viability increases due to the presence of HA and cell proliferation of ≥90% was observed during seven days of cell culture [ 68 ].

Figure  6C  displays SEM images of PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds following three days of culture with L929 and MG63 cells. Among these, the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffold exhibited a well-defined three-dimensional porous structure with interconnected pores, which facilitated cell adhesion and proliferation. The images confirm that cells were able to adhere, infiltrate, and proliferate within the scaffolds, particularly those containing both nHA and VitD 3 .

Similar outcomes were reported by Wei et al. [ 69 ] who evaluated the effects of incorporating hydroxyapatite (HA) microspheres into poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) scaffolds. Their findings showed enhanced adhesion, proliferation, and osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow stem cells (BMSCs) on HA/PLGA scaffolds. Additionally, Sattary et al. [ 70 ] demonstrated that sustained release of VitD 3  in polycaprolactone/gelatin/nHA/VitD 3  scaffolds improved cell attachment and proliferation compared to control scaffolds without VitD 3 . Notably, the VitD 3 -loaded samples showed superior biocompatibility, as well as improved adhesion and cellular spreading on both days 1 and 7 post-culture.

sections.heading: Gene expression
paragraphs: Figure  7  illustrates the relative expression levels of osteogenic genes in MG‑63 cells cultured on the fabricated membranes after 7 days. The expression of COL1A (Fig.  7A ) and RUNX2 (Fig.  7B ) was quantified using qRT‑PCR and normalized to the housekeeping gene GAPDH.

Fig. 7 Relative gene expression of osteogenic markers in MG-63 cells cultured on different membrane formulations after 7 days ( A ) Expression of COL1A and ( B ) Expression of RUNX2. Data are presented as mean values (n = 3) ± standard deviation. Statistical significance is denoted as follows: **P < 0.005, ***P < 0.0005, ****P < 0.00005

The results demonstrated that the presence of bioactive components within the scaffold significantly influenced osteogenic gene expression. As shown in Fig.  7 A, the expression level of COL1A, a major extracellular matrix protein associated with early bone matrix formation, increased in the composite membrane groups compared with the control samples. Among the tested formulations, the membrane containing both nHA and Vit D₃ exhibited the highest COL1A expression, indicating enhanced stimulation of extracellular matrix synthesis. This increase can be attributed to the osteoconductive nature of hydroxyapatite nanoparticles, which provide a biomimetic mineral phase that promotes cell–matrix interactions and supports collagen deposition during early osteogenesis [ 53 ,  71 ].

A similar trend was observed for RUNX2 expression (Fig.  7B ). RUNX2 is a key transcription factor that regulates osteoblast differentiation and plays a central role in initiating osteogenic signaling pathways [ 53 ]. The results revealed a marked upregulation of RUNX2 in cells cultured on membranes containing bioactive additives compared with the pure polymer scaffold. Notably, the PLA/nHA/VitD₃ composite membrane showed the highest RUNX2 expression level, suggesting a synergistic effect between the mineral phase and the osteoinductive molecule. VitD₃ is known to interact with vitamin D receptors (VDRs), activating downstream signaling pathways that regulate osteogenic genes, including RUNX2 and collagen‑related genes. Therefore, its controlled release from the scaffold likely contributed to the enhanced osteogenic response observed in this group [ 52 ,  72 ].

The simultaneous upregulation of RUNX2 and COL1A indicates that the developed composite membranes can effectively support early osteogenic differentiation of MG‑63 cells. RUNX2 activation promotes the transcription of several bone‑related genes, including COL1A, which is responsible for the formation of the organic bone matrix. Consequently, the elevated expression of these markers suggests that the incorporation of nHA and Vit D₃ within the PLA matrix improves the bioactivity of the scaffold and creates a more favorable microenvironment for osteoblast function [ 4 ,  36 ].

Overall, these findings support the hypothesis that the combined incorporation of nano‑hydroxyapatite and Vit D₃ enhances the osteogenic potential of the membrane by promoting both osteogenic transcriptional activity and extracellular matrix formation. Such molecular‑level responses are consistent with the improved cellular behavior observed in the cytocompatibility and morphological analyses, further indicating the suitability of the developed scaffold for bone tissue engineering applications.

sections.heading: In vivo study
paragraphs: We developed models of cranial defects in rabbits to demonstrate the in vivo bone regeneration capability of scaffolds fabricated from PLA. Rabbit calvarial defects were implanted with scaffolds from 4 groups: PLA, PLA/nHA, PLA/nHA-VitD 3 , and a commercial sample. The scaffolds demonstrated excellent tissue compatibility, with no apparent adverse consequences such as foreign body response or inflammation. The reduced inflammatory cell infiltration in VitD 3 -loaded scaffolds is consistent with vitamin D’s immunomodulatory properties, which may contribute to favorable healing.

H&E and Alizarin-red staining were carried out for evaluation of structural and quantitative assessments of new bone formation, the thickness of the connective tissue, immune cells (including neutrophils, lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells) and mineralization in the defective site (Fig.  8 ). It should be noted that Alizarin Red staining was used qualitatively to visualize residual mineralized matrix following controlled decalcification. Although decalcification removes most calcium content, limited mineral-bound structures can remain detectable, enabling assessment of mineralized regions while still permitting paraffin sectioning.

Fig. 8 H&E and Alizarin Red Stain of representative samples from 5 groups.  A  control (H&E staining),  B  control (alizarin staining),  C  PLA (H&E staining),  D  PLA (alizarin staining),  E  PLA/nHA (H&E staining),  F  PLA/nHA (alizarin staining),  G  PLA/nHA-VitD 3 (H&E staining),  H  PLA/nHA-VitD 3  (alizarin staining),  I  Commercial (H&E staining), and ( K ) Commercial (alizarin staining). ( Scale bar  ~  1000 μm )

For negative control, as shown in Fig.  8A , 625 ± 50μm of created bone defected ( ~ 10%) has not been repaired. Despite slow bone regeneration and little new bone formed at the defect site, an ideal inflammatory response was observed. Also, for control groups, Alizarin-red images in Fig.  8B  demonstrated that the unrepaired bone is 1433 ± 34 µm, and the defect size is still present, confirming the H&E staining results. Remarkably, more sponge bone was found in the control group compared to other groups.

As shown in Fig.  8C , using PLA at the defect site, the length of the untreated bone was 1400 ± 34μm (~20%), significantly more than the control group. Also, the analysis of the H&E images showed that by using PLA as a GBR/GTR membrane at the bone defect site, the thickness of the connective tissue increased, and fibrosis was created. According to Fig.  7D , the Alizarin-red image demonstrated that bone islands and the primary bone matrix are forming. However, the unrepaired bone is 5000 ± 58 µm, and the defect area is more than control samples ( ~ 2.5 times).

Furthermore, based on Fig.  8D , it can be said that by adding PLA/nHA to bone defects, bone regeneration has occurred. The length of the untreated bone decreased to 95 ± 10μm, and the difference was significant when compared with the positive control and PLA group (P < 0.05). In addition, loading nHA could significantly enhance bone formation. This issue can be seen in H&E staining and Alizarin-red staining (Fig.  8F ), which demonstrated that the bone matrix is completely formed and the bone is suitable for repair and regeneration.

Similar behaviour can be seen in the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  that showed the length of the untreated bone decreased to 100 ± 9μm, and the bone was treated entirely (Fig.  8G , H). However, the height of the regenerated bone in the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  (~1200μm) was lower than PLA/nHA ( ~ 1400μm), which indicated the favourable effect of the slow release of vitD 3  on the formation of dense bone at the bone defect site. On the other hand, the H&E and alizarin red staining of the commercial sample in Fig.  8 I, K showed that the length of the untreated bone was 2600 ± 55μm (~35%) and these results showed that the amount of untreated bone in the commercial sample is the highest in comparison with other samples. Among these 5 groups, only in PLA/nHA and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  groups, cortical bone could be repaired thoroughly.

Hydroxyapatite, a widely used orthopedic biomaterial in bone repair, could gain more attention due to its enhanced bone regeneration and bioactivity properties [ 73 ]. Similarly, Stevanovic et al. [ 74 ] evaluation of the effect of HA on bone tissue engineering and demonstrated that adding HA to a polyethyleneimine composite scaffold significantly improved bone density and histological characteristics compared to conventional allografts in treating swine’s mandibular defects.

In an additional investigation, Lu et al. [ 75 ] found that incorporating HA into a poly (3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) scaffold promoted the healing of severe bone defects in rabbits with critical-sized radius defects. This treatment also had a notable impact on osteogenic markers such as alkaline phosphate (ALP), osteocalcin (OCN), and mineralized matrix deposits.

On the other hand, VitD 3  is essential for the metabolism of calcium and Phosphorus, as well as activating osteoclasts and osteoblasts to facilitate bone turnover and mineralization [ 76 ]. VitD 3  also influences the immune system, maintaining bone health and healing osseous defects [ 77 ]. By enhancing bone mineral density and improving bone regeneration, studies have shown that releasing VitD 3  and calcium ions at bone defect sites can reduce the risk of bone fracture [ 22 ]. According to another study Osteoclastic activity at grafted sites increased in patients receiving VitD 3 , indicating increased bone turnover and enhanced healing [ 78 ].

Additionally, Mutlu et al. [ 72 ] investigated the impact of sustained VitD 3  release on new bone formation (NBF%) and bone–implant contact (BIC%) values. Their study demonstrated that VitD 3  release over a 9-day period significantly enhanced both NBF% and BIC% around implants placed in box-shaped defects in the sheep iliac crest. Moreover, no signs of inflammation, necrosis, or foreign body reactions were observed, indicating effective osseointegration and biocompatibility of the system.

This study showed that the PLA/nHA-VitD 3  group had considerable new bone formation and the deposition of mature bone-specific extracellular matrix (ECM) in both the edge and central regions. This was attributed to the presence of nHA as a bioactive agent and the sustained release of VitD 3  at the site of the bone defect. The bone tissue regenerated in this group had a suitable height and was more effective than the other groups. The results indicated that successful bone regeneration necessitates biomimetic osteogenic microenvironments. These findings imply that incorporating VitD 3  into nHA-reinforced PLA membranes could shorten healing time and improve outcomes in periodontal and implant surgery. Notably, the PLA/nHA-VitD₃ scaffolds showed far greater osteogenic markers than PLA or PLA/nHA alone. This suggests a synergistic mechanism: nHA provides an osteoconductive surface and releases Ca²⁺/PO₄³⁻ ions, while VitD₃ activates osteogenic signaling pathways, together enhancing bone formation. Similar synergy has been reported in composite scaffolds incorporating hydroxyapatite and vitamin D 3 , where the combination yielded higher osteogenesis than either component alone. A limitation of the present study is the absence of micro‑CT analysis, which could have provided quantitative three‑dimensional information on bone regeneration and defect closure. Future studies will incorporate micro‑CT imaging to strengthen the quantitative assessment of the regenerative outcomes.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: We developed and evaluated PLA, PLA/nHA, and PLA/nHA-VitD 3  GTR/GBR scaffolds in this work. Incorporation of VitD3 significantly reduced fiber diameter, enhanced mechanical properties, and improved hydrophilicity, resulting in favorable degradation and swelling behavior. The combined presence of nHA and VitD3 provided sustained release that supported cell viability, promoted biomineralization, and enabled cortical bone formation in vivo. Osteogenic gene expression analysis further demonstrated increased RUNX2 and COL1A expression in MG‑63 cells cultured on the PLA/nHA‑VitD3 scaffold, supporting its enhanced osteogenic activity at the molecular level. These findings suggest that PLA/nHA-VitD 3  scaffolds hold strong potential for bone tissue engineering applications. Given the clear osteogenic boost in vivo, these membranes could reduce healing times in GTR/GBR procedures. Future work might explore combining VitD₃ with other growth factors or cell types to further enhance outcomes. Overall, the proposed multifunctional PLA/nHA-VitD3 scaffold demonstrates the necessary mechanical integrity and biological activity to serve as a clinically useful GTR/GBR membrane.
